content: Immunological abnormalities may contribute to recurrent miscarriage in some women. As a result, various immunotherapies have been explored as potential treatments for women experiencing recurrent pregnancy loss without an identifiable cause. These therapies include paternal leukocyte immunization and intravenous immunoglobulin. The purpose of this review was to evaluate the effectiveness of different immunotherapies in improving live birth rates among women with a history of unexplained recurrent miscarriages. The review specifically focused on women who had experienced three or more miscarriages, had no more than one live birth, and had no identifiable non-immunological causes for their pregnancy losses. Additionally, no concurrent treatments were allowed in the studies included in the review. To gather relevant data, the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group's Trials Register was searched on February 11, 2014, along with reference lists of studies that were retrieved. Randomized controlled trials that met the inclusion criteria were selected for analysis. Data extraction and quality assessment of the studies were conducted independently by the review author and two co-authors. A total of 20 high-quality trials were included in the review. The results showed no significant differences in live birth rates between women who received immunotherapy and those in the control groups. Specifically: Paternal cell immunization was evaluated in 12 trials involving 641 women. The Peto odds ratio (Peto OR) was 1.23, with a 95% confidence interval (CI) of 0.89 to 1.70, indicating no statistically significant benefit. Third-party donor cell immunization was assessed in three trials with 156 women. The Peto OR was 1.39, with a 95% CI of 0.68 to 2.82, again showing no significant improvement. Trophoblast membrane infusion was studied in one trial involving 37 women. The Peto OR was 0.40, with a 95% CI of 0.11 to 1.45, suggesting no benefit. Intravenous immunoglobulin was examined in eight trials with 303 women. The Peto OR was 0.98, with a 95% CI of 0.61 to 1.58, showing no significant effect. In conclusion, the findings indicate that paternal cell immunization, third-party donor leukocytes, trophoblast membrane infusion, and intravenous immunoglobulin do not provide a significant advantage over placebo in improving live birth rates for women with unexplained recurrent miscarriages.
